newsitem.title: USA: U.S.-S.African discuss trade and development.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-S.African discuss trade and development.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and South African President Thabo Mbeki met on Wednesday to discuss bilateral relations and African trade and development.

"We were discussing with the president the question of what more the United States can and should do with regards to supporting the processes of development on the African continent," Mbeki said after the meeting.
Improving access of African products to U.S. markets and giving multilateral backing for U.S. private investments in Africa would help the continent's development, he said.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the two talked about a broad range of bilateral, regional and global issues, including South Africa's role in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, formerly Zaire.
In addition, the two discussed plans for an anticipated trip by Clinton to Africa, although no date has been set, Mbeki said.
At an earlier meeting on Wednesday of a U.S.-South African commission, defence issues were included for the first time on a list of topics for cooperation between the two governments.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen and South African Defence Minister Joe Modise joined Cabinet colleagues at the session chaired by Mbeki and Vice President Al Gore.

"We believe that as our relationship grows and deepens, it is important and right that we expand the substance of the binational commission to include military and defence-related affairs," Gore said in opening remarks.
The commission, set up three years ago, also discusses cooperation on trade, investment, energy, science and technology, education, the environment and agriculture.
Gore told the one-day meeting at the State Department that cooperation had scored notable successes since the commission last met in Cape Town in February.
South Africa and the United States "worked together successfully to prevent what could have been a massive tragedy as Congo-Kinshasa emerged from the country of Zaire," he said.
New joint business ventures included a partnership between Southwestern Bell Corporation and the South African telephone company Telcom.
Mbeki said there were "no areas of tension in our bilateral relations" and dismissed allegations by what he called "dedicated detractors" of the commission of major rifts between the two countries.

He said the critics' charges related to a compliance programme arising out of settlement of a long-standing arms trade dispute, intellectual property rights affecting U.S. pharmaceutical firms, and relations between Cohen and Modise.
"If they had their way these detractors would have us biting off each other's ears even as I speak here," Mbeki said, to laughter.
